name: finite set with cardinality
essential_semantics: An extensionally or intensionally given finite collection whose size is available and whose elements are unordered and distinct.
rationale: Finite sample spaces, index sets and vocabularies are finite sets; unorderedness and distinctness are semantic, not incidental.

name: sequence indexed by naturals
essential_semantics: An ordered, possibly infinite family with a defined index origin and a rule or listing.
canonical_example: a_n = 1/n for n >= 1
rationale: Sequences underlie limits, series and iterative algorithms; index-origin conventions are a genuine source of error.

name: multiset with multiplicities
essential_semantics: A collection where repetition counts but order does not, distinct from both a set and a sequence.
canonical_example: the multiset of observed values {1, 1, 2}
rationale: Data samples are multisets; representing them as sets loses duplicates and as sequences imposes spurious order.

name: permutation and arrangement
essential_semantics: A bijection of a finite set onto itself or an ordered selection, with composition and inverse available.
canonical_example: the number of permutations of n objects is n!
rationale: Symmetry arguments and exchangeability are permutation statements.

name: unordered selection
essential_semantics: Subsets of a given size, with and without repetition distinguished from ordered arrangements.
canonical_example: choose(n, k) subsets of size k
rationale: The ordered/unordered distinction is exactly what determines the correct count and hence the correct probability.

name: factorial and falling/rising powers
essential_semantics: Standard combinatorial functions on naturals with their conventions (0! = 1) fixed.
canonical_example: n! = product from 1 to n, with 0! = 1
rationale: Small, but a canonical instance where a boundary convention must be pinned rather than assumed.

name: binomial and multinomial coefficients
essential_semantics: Counting function with its domain conditions (0 <= k <= n or the convention of zero outside).
canonical_example: choose(5,2) = 10
rationale: It appears in every discrete distribution and its out-of-range convention affects computed probabilities.

name: summation with an explicit index and range
essential_semantics: Binds an index over a stated range or index set, including empty-range conventions and multi-index sums.
canonical_example: sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i, with the empty sum equal to 0
rationale: Summation is the most frequent binder in applied mathematics after quantifiers; the index set is semantic content, not syntax.

name: indexed product
essential_semantics: Binds an index and multiplies, with the empty-product convention and non-commutative cases handled by preserving order.
canonical_example: product_{i=1}^{n} p(x_i), empty product equal to 1
rationale: Likelihoods are indexed products; ordering matters when the factors are matrices.

name: indexed maximum, minimum and argmax over a finite set
essential_semantics: Extremum over an index set with ties and emptiness handled explicitly.
canonical_example: argmax_{i in I} score_i, undefined for empty I
rationale: Ties and empty ranges are real cases that a representation must be able to state rather than silently resolve.

name: recurrence relation with initial conditions
essential_semantics: A defining relation over an index with the required number of initial values, distinct from a closed form.
rationale: Recurrences with insufficient initial conditions do not define a sequence; the count is a checkable condition.

name: generating function
essential_semantics: A formal power series encoding a sequence, where formal manipulation is distinguished from analytic convergence.
canonical_example: sum a_n x^n as a formal series
rationale: The formal/analytic distinction is a real one that a representation should not collapse.

name: graph as vertices plus edges
essential_semantics: A vertex set with an edge relation, with simplicity, loops and multi-edges declared.
canonical_example: G = (V, E) with E a set of unordered pairs
rationale: Graph structure is a mathematical object with variants that change every theorem about it.

name: directed graph
essential_semantics: Edges as ordered pairs, with in/out degree and direction preserved by all operations.
canonical_example: an edge from u to v does not imply one from v to u
rationale: Causal and dependency structures are directed; losing direction is a total loss of the causal claim.

name: directed acyclic graph with acyclicity as a checked property
essential_semantics: A directed graph with no directed cycles, where acyclicity is verified rather than assumed.
canonical_example: a Bayesian network structure
rationale: Generative models and causal graphs must be acyclic to define a joint distribution; a cycle silently invalidates the model.

name: weighted and labelled graphs
essential_semantics: Edge or vertex attributes with their own types and possibly units.
canonical_example: edge weights in kilometres
rationale: Network optimisation attaches typed quantities to edges; untyped weights admit unit errors.

name: paths, reachability and connectivity
essential_semantics: Walks, paths and cycles distinguished; reachability as a relation derived from the edge relation.
canonical_example: there is a directed path from X to Y
rationale: Backdoor criteria and dependency analysis are path statements.

name: tree and rooted hierarchy
essential_semantics: Acyclic connected graph, possibly rooted with parent/child structure.
canonical_example: a decision tree or a nested grouping structure
rationale: Nested experimental designs and hierarchical indices are trees.

name: matrix representation of a graph
essential_semantics: A matrix view of a graph where the vertex ordering is an arbitrary choice and results should be order-invariant.
canonical_example: A_{ij} = 1 iff (i,j) in E
rationale: One object with two views (combinatorial and matrix) is a clean test of multi-representation support.

name: matchings, covers and independent sets
essential_semantics: Combinatorial substructures defined by constraints, whose optimisation versions are standard problems.
canonical_example: a maximum matching in a bipartite graph
rationale: Canonical combinatorial optimisation objects requiring constraint expression over discrete structures.

name: network flow with conservation constraints
essential_semantics: Edge-indexed variables with per-vertex conservation and capacity constraints.
canonical_example: max flow subject to conservation at every internal node
rationale: Indexed constraint families over a graph structure exercise scoped constraint generation.

name: partitions and colourings
essential_semantics: Assignments of labels subject to constraints, with the partition of a set as a derived object.
canonical_example: a proper 3-colouring assigns different colours to adjacent vertices
rationale: Constraint satisfaction over discrete labels, a standard hardness benchmark.

name: partial order and incomparability
essential_semantics: A reflexive antisymmetric transitive relation in which two elements may be incomparable, distinct from a total order.
canonical_example: subset inclusion is a partial order; {1} and {2} are incomparable
rationale: Incomparability is a positive fact, not missing information; Pareto dominance and type lattices depend on it.

name: lattice with meet and join
essential_semantics: A partial order with binary greatest lower and least upper bounds, used for type joins and abstract domains.
canonical_example: the meet of Probability and PositiveReal is NonNegativeReal
rationale: Type unification and static analysis are lattice computations; without meets, incomparable types cannot be combined principledly.

name: Boolean algebra and normal forms
essential_semantics: Complemented distributive lattice with canonical normal forms (CNF, DNF) available.
canonical_example: conversion of a formula to conjunctive normal form
rationale: Normal forms are the canonicalisation story for propositional content.

name: automaton / labelled transition system
essential_semantics: States, transitions and acceptance, with determinism declared.
canonical_example: a DFA accepting strings with an even number of a's
rationale: Included as the discrete-dynamics counterpart to Markov chains, marking a domain boundary.

name: formal language and grammar
essential_semantics: Sets of strings defined by a grammar, with ambiguity of the grammar itself a meaningful property.
canonical_example: a context-free grammar and whether it is ambiguous
rationale: Relevant to any system that must reason about its own or another notation's grammar.

name: computational cost as a mathematical statement
essential_semantics: A cost function of input size with the machine model and the measured resource stated.
canonical_example: sorting requires Omega(n log n) comparisons
rationale: A cost claim without a model or resource is not falsifiable.

name: complexity classes and reductions
essential_semantics: Classes of problems with reductions between them as the structuring relation.
canonical_example: 3-SAT is NP-complete
rationale: Included to mark the boundary between mathematical statements about problems and statements within them.

name: combinatorial identity with validity range
essential_semantics: Identities among counting expressions with the range of indices for which they hold.
canonical_example: sum_k choose(n,k) = 2^n for n >= 0
rationale: Universally quantified identities over a discrete domain, the natural target of induction.

name: counting principles as reusable arguments
essential_semantics: Inclusion-exclusion, pigeonhole and bijective counting stated as principles with hypotheses.
canonical_example: if n items go into k < n boxes, some box has two items
rationale: Discrete existence proofs are counting arguments; representing the principle makes the reasoning explicit.
